requirement_title: Add ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute to generated code.
requirement_text:
# REQ-2297: Add ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute to generated code.

Source: https://github.com/MessagePack-CSharp/MessagePack-CSharp/issues/2297
Type: feature

## Requirement

MessagePack generated code is not decorated with the `ExcludeFromCodeCoverage` attribute. Because it is very hard to write good coverage for generated MessagePack code, it may skew coverage numbers, especially on large projects with a lot of generated code.

Solution requested: "I would like all generated code to be decorated with ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute.  I do not feel like a setting is needed, but setting would be fine to have too."

Alternatives considered by the author: none; "it is close to impossible to write good coverage for generated code as it covers many edge cases."

## Acceptance criteria

- All generated code is decorated with `ExcludeFromCodeCoverage`.
- No new setting or option is required to get the attribute. ("I do not feel like a setting is needed")
- An opt-out setting would be acceptable but is optional. ("setting would be fine to have too")
- The generated code still compiles on every supported target framework (the attribute must exist there or be conditionally emitted). (derived)
- Existing verified generator snapshots are updated to include the attribute. (derived)

## Notes from discussion

- b-kurczynski-dl suggests a coverage-tool workaround instead: exclude `obj\\.*\.g\.cs$` in the `dotnet-coverage` settings XML.
- armadavalor offers a PR: add `[global::System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` (and possibly `GeneratedCode`) to the types emitted by the templates under `src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/Transforms/` (formatters, string-key formatters, enum/union formatters, resolvers), update the verified snapshots, no setting. Asks AArnott whether he would accept it or prefer to point users at coverage-tool configuration. No maintainer reply in the thread.
- Ambiguity driver: scope (all generated types vs formatters only) and setting (unconditional vs opt-out) are both open.
verdict_reason: verified high finding(s) backed by receipts: requirement-tests-1, logic-edge-1

checked.what: Existing SourceGenerator tests on head: 168/169 passed, 1 failed
Existing SourceGenerator tests on base: 167/167 passed, 0 failed
Receipts/ExcludeFromCodeCoverageDefaultTests.cs: requirement test fails on base (1/1), passes on head (1/1)
Receipts/ExcludeFromCodeCoverageTfmTests.cs: edge-case test fails on head: 2/2 failed
Receipts/ExcludeFromCodeCoverageDuplicateTests.cs: edge-case test fails on head: 1/1 failed
Regeneration: 219/222 generated files verified by 89 passing snapshot tests on head; 1 head test(s) fail

findings.claim: The requirement asks for all generated code to carry `ExcludeFromCodeCoverage`, but every template wraps the attribute in `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`. Projects targeting netstandard2.0 or any .NET Framework TFM therefore get undecorated formatters and resolvers. The attribute is available on both: netstandard2.0 exposes `System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute`, and .NET Framework 4.0+ has it in mscorlib with AttributeUsage that includes Class. So the derived criterion ('the attribute must exist there or be conditionally emitted') does not justify excluding these targets. netstandard2.0 is the most common library target, so a large share of users get no benefit.

receipt_plan.detail: Run tests/MessagePack.SourceGenerator.Tests/Receipts/ExcludeFromCodeCoverageTfmTests.cs. With the NETSTANDARD2_0 or NETFRAMEWORK preprocessor symbol set, generated formatter and resolver classes have no active ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute, so the test fails on head. As a second check, compile a netstandard2.0 class library carrying `[System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` on a class: it builds with no error, which shows the guard is unnecessary. (generated tests: GeneratedCode_IsExcludedFromCodeCoverage_OnAllTargetFrameworks)

findings.claim: The generated resolver is a `partial class` that completes a user-written declaration (`[GeneratedMessagePackResolver] partial class MyResolver { }`). The generated half now always carries `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]`, and that attribute has AllowMultiple=false. A user who already put `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` on their own partial declaration therefore gets CS0579 'Duplicate ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute' and the project no longer compiles. Users following the issue's workaround advice are exactly the ones likely to have done this, so this is a breaking change. The same applies to the CompositeResolverTemplate partial class.

receipt_plan.detail: Run Receipts.GeneratedTests.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageDuplicateTests.UserResolverAlreadyExcludedFromCoverage_CompilesWithoutDuplicateAttribute. The source declares `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage][GeneratedMessagePackResolver] partial class MyResolver {}` plus one [MessagePackObject] type and expects no diagnostics. It passes on base and fails on head with CS0579 in the generated MyResolver file.

hunches.claim: The attribute is wrapped in `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`, but this conditional is evaluated in the consuming project's compilation. ExcludeFromCodeCoverage exists in netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework 4.0+ (mscorlib), so the guard needlessly skips users on those targets. Those users still get the coverage skew the requirement describes, so 'all generated code' is not met for them. Separately, projects targeting netstandard2.1 or net6+ are covered, while multi-targeting projects get inconsistent output across TFMs.

receipt_plan.detail: Compile generated output in a project targeting net48 and netstandard2.0. Assert the formatter type carries ExcludeFromCodeCoverage via reflection or Roslyn symbol inspection. It will fail because the #if removes the attribute. Compare with a net8.0 build.

hunches.claim: The attribute is not applied to every generated type or member. Only the formatter, resolver and nested cache/helper classes are decorated. Other generated code, such as the GetFormatterHelper static dictionary and any additional generated helper types, may be undecorated. The requirement says 'all generated code'.

receipt_plan.detail: Rerun the snapshot tests, then scan the generated snapshot outputs for type declarations (class/struct/enum) lacking a preceding ExcludeFromCodeCoverage. Also check any other templates or emitters in Transforms/ for undecorated types.

hunches.claim: The `#if` / `#endif` lines are emitted at column 0, inside `EmitNestingTypesAndNamespaces`. If a user's generated file or a custom emitter later wraps this output (for example in a `#nullable` or `#pragma` context), the output formatting and checked-in snapshots change for every type. Users who check in generator output will see a diff in all 222 snapshots without opting in.

receipt_plan.detail: Run the generator snapshot tests at base and head and diff the outputs. Confirm that every generated file differs only by the added #if/attribute/#endif lines.

hunches.claim: Only the top-level types and the nested FormatterCache and GetFormatterHelper classes are decorated. The requirement says 'all generated code'. Any other generated type or file not routed through these templates, for example the resolver's other helper types, is not covered. The test only checks that each file contains the attribute at least once, not that every generated type has it.

receipt_plan.detail: Add a test that parses each generated tree, enumerates all type declarations, and asserts that each has ExcludeFromCodeCoverage under the guard. Run it against the head build.

hunches.claim: The test asserts only that the ExcludeFromCodeCoverage text appears somewhere in each generated file. FormatterCache<T> and GetFormatterHelper are nested types in the resolver, so deleting the attribute on one of them does not fail the file-level Contains check. The guard test compares the attribute count with the guarded count, which also survives the deletion because the remaining attributes are still guarded.

receipt_plan.detail: src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/Transforms/ResolverTemplate.tt:31 delete-statement: remove the ExcludeFromCodeCoverage block on FormatterCache<T> (and on GetFormatterHelper) -> expected to survive because the resolver class itself still carries the attribute and the tests only check Contains and count equality per file. Run CodeCoverageExclusionTests.

hunches.claim: The guard test checks the text of the #if guard but never compiles the generated code with NETSTANDARD2_0 or NETFRAMEWORK defined, nor on a TFM lacking the attribute. The generated code is not compiled at all in these tests. An incorrect guard symbol that still matches the string is not caught. A wrong or missing guard in a template, for example on a path the test source does not exercise, would also go unnoticed.

receipt_plan.detail: CompositeResolverTemplate.tt:7 negate-condition: change `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK` to `#if NETSTANDARD2_0` -> the string-matching guard test fails only because of the literal text. A semantic mutation such as renaming the symbol in both the template and the test constant would survive, because no compilation under netstandard2.0 is done.

hunches.claim: The test source never exercises generic formatters, nested types, or the CompositeResolver template, since there is no [CompositeResolver] usage. The CompositeResolverTemplate changes (class and FormatterCache) therefore have no direct test other than the snapshot regeneration. Removing the attribute there would not fail the new tests.

receipt_plan.detail: src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/Transforms/CompositeResolverTemplate.cs:27 delete-statement: remove the ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute from the Write string -> expected to survive CodeCoverageExclusionTests because TestSource has no composite resolver; only the snapshot tests would notice.

hunches.claim: The README says the attribute 'is only emitted for targets where it is available (not `netstandard2.0` or .NET Framework)'. This is factually wrong: `ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute` exists in netstandard2.0 and in .NET Framework 4.0+. The docs misstate why those targets are left out of the requirement.

receipt_plan.detail: Check the netstandard2.0 reference assembly (NETStandard.Library 2.0 ref/netstandard.dll) and the .NET Framework 4.x mscorlib for System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute. It is present in both, which contradicts README.md:1639-1640.

hunches.claim: Every emitted attribute is wrapped in `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`. `System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute` exists in .NET Framework 4.0+ and in netstandard2.0, and class targets are allowed there. As a result, consumers targeting netstandard2.0 or net472 (both MessagePack-supported targets and very common for libraries) get no attribute on any generated type, even though it would compile. The requirement is that all generated code be decorated, and the derived criterion only allows conditional emission where the attribute does not exist.

receipt_plan.detail: The guard `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK` appears in all six templates (FormatterTemplate.tt:14, StringKeyFormatterTemplate.tt:18, EnumTemplate.tt:8, UnionTemplate.tt:10, ResolverTemplate.tt:14/31/48, CompositeResolverTemplate.tt:7/35). Confirm the attribute exists in netstandard2.0 and net472 reference assemblies, e.g. by compiling `[System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] class C{}` against ReferenceAssemblies.NetStandard.NetStandard20 and NetFramework.Net472.

hunches.claim: The attribute is emitted only under `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`, so generated code in consumers targeting netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework (a common MessagePack target) gets no exclusion. The requirement says ALL generated code should be decorated. The guard is a deliberate compile-safety choice, but it leaves a coverage gap. The README documents it.

receipt_plan.detail: Read the `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK` guards in the templates. Compile a netstandard2.0 or net472 consumer with the generator and observe that no ExcludeFromCodeCoverage is emitted. Note that on net472 the attribute does exist in mscorlib, so the NETFRAMEWORK guard looks overly broad.

hunches.claim: The README sentence is placed in the custom-formatter mixing section, which is an odd location for generated-code behavior. The change adds no opt-out setting and does not mention one. Neither the requirement nor the ledger says whether an opt-out is wanted.

receipt_plan.detail: Review README.md around line 1639 for a more suitable section, such as the source generator or analyzer docs.

refused.what: Which reading of REQ-2297 is intended (A or B)
refused.why: 3 of 3 independent readers found two readings: A: Unconditionally add [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] to every type the source generator emits (formatters, enum/union formatters, resolvers, string-key formatters, etc.), with no setting; B: Add the attribute to all generated types by default, plus provide an opt-out setting (e.g. MSBuild property or MessagePackKnownFormatter/GeneratorOptions flag) to disable it; the requirement says: 'I would like all generated code to be decorated with ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute. I do not feel like a setting is needed, but setting would be fine to have too'.

residual_risk: This change touches 236 files (222 generated) in codegen-templates, tests; the highest routed risk is 7/10. 13 file(s) were routed for deep review, 1 for light review and 222 to the regeneration check. The existing source generator tests ran on head: 168 of 169 passed, 1 failed. 11 unverified hunch(es) remain without an executed receipt. It touches risky areas (codegen-templates), so a human must sign off. 6 thing(s) were not checked, including mutation testing; generated formatter bytes (source generator output, base vs head); compatibility byte diff (base vs head serialized bytes). By signing off, the signer accepts any defect that only those unchecked paths would have revealed. The change is blocked; signing off is not offered until the blocker is fixed.

interpretations.label: A
interpretations.summary: Unconditionally add [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] to every type the source generator emits (formatters, enum/union formatters, resolvers, string-key formatters, etc.), with no setting. Code: Edit all templates under Transforms/ to emit the attribute on every generated type, always, with no MSBuild property or option; update all snapshots.

interpretations.label: B
interpretations.summary: Add the attribute to all generated types by default, plus provide an opt-out setting (e.g. MSBuild property or MessagePackKnownFormatter/GeneratorOptions flag) to disable it. Code: Adds a new public configuration option, reads it in the generator, and conditionally emits the attribute in templates; the other reading adds no option.
